input.question: Why can extreme hot weather cause mass power outages/blackouts?
input.ground_truth: The main reason is that electricity usage is highest during heat waves, because everyone's air conditioning is running at full blast. There's a second less important reason, which is that fossil fuel and nuclear power plants are less efficient in hot weather. They use outside air and/or water to cool their steam back to water to recycle back into the plant, and that doesn't work as well on a hot day. In fact, it turns out there's a theorem of thermodynamics that says that the maximum possible efficiency of both heat engines (power plant) and refrigerators (air conditioners) is worse when the outside air is warmer. _URL_0_

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why can extreme hot weather cause mass power outages/blackouts?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine it’s a super, super hot day, and everyone wants their air conditioner to stay on so they don’t get too hot.

When it’s very hot, lots of people turn on their air conditioners at the same time. Air conditioners need a lot of electricity to work. If too many people use electricity at once, it’s like too many kids trying to drink from the same tiny cup—there’s not enough to go around!

Also, some power plants that make electricity get their water from rivers or lakes to stay cool. But if it’s super hot, the water might not be cool enough, or there might not be enough water because everyone is using it. So, the power plant can’t make electricity as well, or it has to turn off to stay safe.

That’s why, on very hot days, sometimes the electricity goes out for everyone—that’s called a blackout or power outage.
